title: Pythonic getting and setting for externaly configurable attributes?
author: DocTrucker
hprodh
text:
I’d think the first best advice is to follow the API as it is designed for, or in the way it is most used  by other users, so that your code is coherent with standard usage.
Then yes setting an attribute might feel more convenient because of the auto-completion, code introspection, etc… (The string might have a typo that will silently pass)
My personal favourite is to have a general set function that takes kwargs
external_device.set(external_estop=True, value=1)

This is flexible because you can also create dicts and pass them as kwargs, also possibly combine them with dict union operator
default_conf = {
    "external_estop": False,
    "value": 1,
}
spec_conf = {"external_estop": True}

...

external_device.set(**(default_conf | spec_conf))

author: AlSweigart
text:
Wesley Brooks:

external_device.external_estop = True


I think the getters/setters approach is probably best. I doubt you’ll block access to other class or inherited attributes.
I think the term you’re thinking of is properties, rather than decorators. Properties are how Python automatically turns an assignment statement into a setter function call behind the scenes, and turns attribute access into a getter function call.
Creating set_value() and get_value() methods is generally not “pythonic”, but pythonic-ness isn’t a hard requirement.

author: petercordia
text:
Generally, communication with other devices or programs should not happen inside getters, setters, __init__ or __new__. This is ‘just’ a convention, so it is quite possible there are groups of people that have other conventions.
I would favour either the interface
external_decice.set_external_estop(True)

or
external_device.set(external_estop=True)

(depending on details.)

author: DocTrucker
text:
Thanks for the comments. It looks like it’s largely dealers choice!
The issue is there are over 500 parameters. I’ve been supplied a cvs file which I’m manipulating into a configuration file. However, unless I’m missing a trick hard coding 500+ set and get functions is impractical & begging for long hidden errors.
I suppose I could generate a core function for get/set for each data type and then create functions at runtime in the program?

author: Rosuav
text:
Wesley Brooks:

Thanks for the comments. It looks like it’s largely dealers choice!


Welcome to design decisions. Almost nothing is “right” or “wrong”. You get to pick, but with the understanding that your choice of API will heavily affect your users’ expectations.
One thing to be aware of: If you use external_device.external_estop = True, you risk someone writing external_device.extrnal_estop = True and having it silently do nothing. So you would need to guard against that. Coupled with the general expectation that this sort of syntax should be fast (not triggering lengthy external operations), I would recommend having a method call. The kwargs style works well, particularly if you can guarantee atomicity (if calling set(foo=1, bar=2) is guaranteed to apply both changes simultaneously - this depends on the device, of course), and it still allows you to set more than one.
Having a generic set_value(attr, type, value) method call would be a good fallback for people whose devices might not be fully recognized. You can have a recommended (“normal”) API that uses kwargs, does full automatic type conversions (if you pass 5 to something that’s expecting a boolean, it automatically sends True), and catches any misspelled keywords (raising an exception if something isn’t recognized), but the low-level API can provide direct access when needed.
For an example of how this might look, I’m going to grab a third-party high level library but a stdlib low-level one. To manipulate a webcam in Linux, I can use this:
from linuxpy.video.device import Device
with Device("/dev/video0") as fd:
    print("Current focus:", fd.controls.focus_absolute.value)

or I can do this:
fcntl.ioctl(fd, IOC.S_CTRL, raw.v4l2_control(id, value))

which is what’s happening deep inside the .value getter and setter. The low level API is a pain to use, but most of the time, the high level API is what people will use.

author: DocTrucker
text:
Chris Angelico:

One thing to be aware of: If you use external_device.external_estop = True, you risk someone writing external_device.extrnal_estop = True and having it silently do nothing.


That’ll be the nail in the coffin for the obj.varaible_name = variable approach. Sometimes the obvious needs to be stated!
The calls shouldn’t be too laggy. The code will be using a thread to do the networking. It will continually read the whole data area to a set of files which will sit on a ram drive. Reads will read from these copies of the external devices memory area and writes will be queued to be carried out between the block reads. There are two copies of most parameters, write to one and the external device writes to the second to acknowledge the parameter change.
Good call on the low level access option.
